analysis.title: Asia Economics Analyst: China's High-Tech Push: Support for Output, Less for Employment
key_insights: High-tech sectors (high-tech manufacturing including pharmaceuticals and equipment, new energy vehicles, and telecom, IT and software services) accounted for 38% of industrial production in 2025, up from 33% in 2021. Their share of total fixed asset investment rose from 13% to 18.4% over the same period.

High-tech sectors directly accounted for 16.4% of GDP in value-added terms in 2025, about 6pp more than a decade earlier. Including upstream spillovers, they account for 23% of GDP in 2026, above the property sector's 15% share.

Employment share of high-tech sectors rose only from 10.4% in 2018 to 10.8% in 2023 (latest data), reflecting capital-intensive production. Computer and communications equipment manufacturing is the largest in production and investment but only 2.5% of employment. Telecom, IT and software services is the largest in employment at 2.7%.

Every RMB100 of final spending on high-tech goods and services generates about RMB73 of domestic value added, versus RMB90 for property and RMB92 for services. The gap reflects higher reliance on imported inputs, so more spending leaks abroad.

Every RMB100 of high-tech final spending generates about RMB33 of labor compensation, versus RMB40 for property and RMB46 for services. Versus property, the gap comes from import leakage, since workers in both receive about 45% of domestic value added. Services directs roughly 50% of domestic value added to workers.

Each RMB1mn of final spending supports about 3 jobs in high-tech, versus 4.6 in property and 4.4 in services overall. High-tech expansion can support GDP growth without a proportionate gain in household income and consumption.

High-tech demand is investment- and export-led. Only about 20% of spending on high-tech products comes from household and government consumption, versus roughly 70% for services. Nearly half comes from investment purchases and about a third from exports. Exports are nearly half of final demand within high-tech manufacturing.

A shift in activity from property to high-tech gives exports a larger role in China's growth outlook and does not by itself require a shift to consumption-led growth. GS says this reliance may partly explain policymakers' lackluster support for household consumption.

High-tech manufacturing's share of nominal goods exports rose about 4pp between 2018 and 2025, and gross exports rose about 2pp of GDP. The share rose further in 2026, mainly because of higher prices from AI-related inflation in those sectors.

GS estimates high-tech sectors contributed about 1.9pp a year to real GDP growth in 2016-25 and expects a broadly stable contribution of about 2pp a year in 2026-30. It expects their direct GDP share to rise to around 28% by 2030.

The property sector's GDP share has fallen to around 15% after five years of sharp contraction, versus 25-30% in 2016. GS expects it to stabilize near 8% from 2030. The property downturn is likely to persist, but its drag should fade. The combined growth impulse from high-tech and property should turn increasingly positive in 2027-30.

GS estimates Six Networks investment (water, power grids, computing, communications, urban underground pipelines, logistics) at RMB28.4tn in the 15th FYP (2026-30), up 14% from RMB24.9tn in the 14th FYP, or 2.7% annualized growth.
Data center build-out could add about 40bp to the average level of China's real GDP in 2026-30. The full RMB28.4tn Six Networks investment could add about 4% to the average GDP level.

China is expected to account for nearly 20% of global data-center capacity additions in 2025-30, per GS equity analysts. A growing share of capacity is for AI inference, so computing hardware is a larger share of data-center spending. Local chip sourcing should limit import leakage and raise the domestic growth multiplier.

Rising self-sufficiency in areas such as semiconductors will lift the domestic value-added share of high-tech over time. Reducing import reliance is likely one reason for policymakers' push for home-grown high-tech.

sector_views.rationale: Expected to contribute about 2pp a year to real GDP growth in 2026-30 and rise to about 28% of GDP directly by 2030, supported by constructive real export outlook and AI compute demand.
Downturn likely to persist, but the drag fades as GDP share falls from 25-30% in 2016 to about 15% now and about 8% from 2030.

risk_factors: Higher export dependence of high-tech sectors increases exposure to foreign demand.
Property downturn is likely to persist, though its drag diminishes.
High-tech growth delivers limited employment and household income gains, which may keep consumption weak.
Part of the 2026 rise in high-tech export share reflects AI-related price inflation rather than volume.
charts_described: Exhibit 2 title states high-tech sectors account for 38% of industrial production and 18% of investment but only 11% of employment.

geopolitical: Intensifying technology competition with the US is making China's push for technological self-reliance more urgent.
China requires at least 80% of infrastructure and AI chips in its nationwide network of AI data centers to be sourced from domestic suppliers, as reported by Bloomberg.
The July Politburo meeting called for progress on the Six Networks, and a late-September State Council meeting urged an accelerated start to major projects.

tension_points.bull_case: High-tech sectors contribute about 2pp a year to real GDP growth in 2026-30 and rise to about 28% of GDP by 2030, while the property drag fades as its share falls to around 8%, so the combined impulse turns positive in 2027-30.
tension_points.bear_case: High-tech growth is capital-intensive and import-reliant. It creates fewer domestic value added, labor income and jobs per yuan than property or services, so it supports GDP without a proportionate gain in household income and consumption.

theme_stances.key_argument: High-tech sectors should contribute about 2pp a year to GDP growth in 2026-30 while the property drag fades.
theme_stances.evidence: broadly stable contribution of around 2pp annually in 2026–30
